title: Survival
about: Disaster, field craft, food, water, power and repair references. Mostly Kiwix books plus a few primary source manuals from the agencies that wrote them.

items.note: USDA Complete Guide to Home Canning.

items.title: EPA: Emergency Disinfection of Drinking Water
Nuclear War Survival Skills (Kearny, Oak Ridge National Laboratory)
Survival (US Army ATP 3-50.21): water, food, fire, shelter, medicine, navigation
items.note: The Army's current survival manual, approved for public release. Start here.

items.title: Wild Edibles of Missouri (Jan Phillips, Missouri Department of Conservation)
items.note: Midwest. 243 pages of edible wild plants with drawings and recipes. Most of these plants grow across the eastern half of North America.

items.title: Useful Wild Plants of the United States and Canada (Charles Francis Saunders, 1920)
items.note: The whole country in one book, strongest on California and the Southwest. Roots, seeds, nuts, berries, greens, drinks, soap and medicine plants, with drawings and a chapter on poisonous ones. Plant names are those of 1920.

items.title: Food Plants of the North American Indians (Elias Yanovsky, USDA, 1936)
items.note: A list of 1,112 plants eaten across the United States and Canada: which part, how it was prepared and where. No pictures. Use it to learn what grows in your region, then identify each plant with a picture guide before you trust it.

items.title: Facts on Edible Wild Greens in Maine (University of Maine Cooperative Extension)
items.note: Northeast. Dandelions, fiddleheads, lamb's quarters, orache and purslane: how to pick them and cook them.

items.title: Iroquois Uses of Maize and Other Food Plants (Arthur C. Parker, New York State Museum, 1910)
items.note: Northeast. How the Iroquois of New York grew, stored and cooked corn, beans and squash, and the wild greens, fungi, fruits, nuts, saps and roots they ate beside them.

items.title: Uses of Plants by the Chippewa Indians (Frances Densmore, Smithsonian, 1928)
items.note: Great Lakes and the northern woods. Plants the Chippewa of Minnesota used for food and medicine, wild rice and maple sugar among them.

items.title: Forgotten Foods: Introduction to Wild Edible Plants (Mississippi State University Extension)
items.license: Free to copy unchanged for nonprofit teaching, with credit
items.note: Southeast. Four pages on the rules of safe foraging, with a table of common wild food plants and which part of each is eaten.

items.title: Edible and Poisonous Plants of the Caribbean Region (US Navy, 1944)
items.note: Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands. Drawings of tropical food plants and of the poisonous ones. Many of the same plants grow in south Florida and Hawaii.

items.title: Uses of Plants by the Indians of the Missouri River Region (Melvin R. Gilmore, Smithsonian, 1919)
items.note: Great Plains. Plants the Dakota, Omaha, Ponca and Pawnee used for food and medicine, with photographs.

items.title: Culturally Significant Plants (USDA NRCS Plant Materials Center, Manhattan, Kansas)
items.license: US government work, photos credited inside
items.note: Great Plains and the eastern states. About 80 plants, one to a page, with a photo and the food, medicine and craft uses of each. It says which ones are poisonous unless prepared.

items.title: Preserving Food in Wyoming (University of Wyoming Extension, 2018)
items.note: Rocky Mountains and High Plains. The wild fruit chapter covers chokecherry, wild plum, serviceberry, rose hips, buffaloberry, currants, gooseberries, wild grapes and prickly pear. The rest is a full home canning manual written for high altitude.

items.title: Desert Foods for a Resilient Future (University of Arizona Desert Laboratory, 2021)
items.note: Southwest deserts. Mesquite, prickly pear, cholla buds, agave, wild chile, amaranth, purslane and tepary beans: how to harvest and cook each, with cautions.

items.title: The Ethno-Botany of the Coahuilla Indians of Southern California (David Prescott Barrows, 1900)
items.note: Southern California desert and mountains. How the Cahuilla gathered, prepared and stored mesquite, agave, yucca, cactus, acorns, pine nuts, palm fruit and chia.

items.title: Guide to Island Chumash Plant Usage (Channel Islands National Park)
items.note: California coast. Plant foods and medicines of the Island Chumash, among them acorns, island cherry, chia, red maids and toyon.

items.title: Special Forest Products: Species Information Guide for the Pacific Northwest (US Forest Service, 2001)
items.note: Oregon and Washington; many of the species also grow in Alaska, northern Idaho and western Montana. About 60 forest plants and mushrooms that people gather, with harvest notes. Food, medicine and craft plants sit together, so read each entry: not everything in it is edible.

items.title: Wildflowers of the National Forests in Alaska (US Forest Service)
items.note: Coastal Alaska. Pocket guide to common flowers and berries of the Tongass and Chugach forests. Several entries are marked edible or poisonous.

items.title: Emergency Food Plants and Poisonous Plants of the Islands of the Pacific (War Department TM 10-420, 1943)
items.note: Pacific islands. Drawings of the food plants and the poisonous plants, with how to prepare each. Many of the same plants grow in Hawaii, Guam and American Samoa.

items.title: A Guide to Missouri's Edible and Poisonous Mushrooms (Missouri Department of Conservation)
items.note: Never eat a mushroom you cannot name with certainty.

items.title: Plants Poisonous to Livestock in the Western States (USDA Agricultural Research Service)
items.note: Written for stock keepers. The same plants poison people.

items.title: North American Trapper Education Manual (Association of Fish and Wildlife Agencies)
Care of Game: field dressing and storing meat (Connecticut Hunter Safety Manual)
Basic Fishing: tackle, knots, where fish live, cleaning the catch (Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources)
Drinking Water, Sanitation and Hygiene in Emergencies: 15 technical notes (WHO and WEDC)
items.note: Note 5 covers making water safe where you use it. Others cover cleaning wells and tanks, how much water people need, and latrines.

items.title: Basic Land Navigation: maps, compass and GPS (National Wildfire Coordinating Group, PMS 475)
Star wheel for latitude 40 north (planisphere kit, Dominic Ford)
items.note: Print, cut out and pin together. It shows which stars are up at any date and hour, so the sky tells you the hour when you know the date, or the date when you know the hour. Take the wheel nearest your latitude.
